Electric power distribution is the delivery system of electricity to places that use it, such as homes and other buildings. It is done mainly by power lines, transformers, substations and meters. The electricity comes from the power station at high voltage and is delivered at medium to low voltage levels.
In early days, electricity was distributed as direct current (DC). Alternating current (AC) was later introduced during the War of Currents. DC distribution disappeared because transformers can easily convert AC to high voltage for electric power transmission and low voltage to use at home.

Restoring the old workshop took most of the winter. The building had stood empty since the mill closed, and damp had crept into every corner of the long room. We began by clearing the debris: broken chairs, rusted tins, a heap of newspapers from a decade nobody remembered. The floorboards were soft in places, so we lifted them one by one and laid new joists beneath, working slowly because the ceiling above us sagged and the plaster crumbled whenever we knocked against it. My uncle had spent thirty years in that room, and he insisted on doing the work in the order he had been taught: first the roof, then the walls, then the benches. He was patient with the roof and less patient with the benches, which is why the benches took longer.

By February the structure was sound and we could turn to the fittings. The north bench was built from oak that had been stacked in the yard for years, and when we planed it the grain opened up like a map. We joined the legs with dowels rather than screws, because my uncle distrusted screws. Along the back wall we installed a steel rack for the tools, and beside it a sheet of glass on which he could sketch measurements with a wax pencil. The old brass handles from the cabinet doors were cleaned in vinegar and put back where they belonged. A copper pipe ran from the sink to the drain, green with age, and we replaced the section under the window because it had cracked.

The work was not glamorous. Most days we ate sandwiches on the step and listened to the rain. Neighbours stopped by to ask what we were doing and stayed to talk about the mill, the river, the price of timber. In March a historian from the county office came to look at the roof beams and told us they were older than the building itself, salvaged from a church that had burned down. He took notes in a small book and promised to send us a copy of his report, which never arrived.

By the time spring came the room smelled of sawdust and varnish. My uncle swept the floor every evening, even when we had done nothing all day, and he would stand at the door and look at the benches as though checking them against some plan in his head. I asked him once whether he was satisfied, and he said that a workshop is never finished, only abandoned.
